title: Mount Fuji Climbing Season Opens
paragraphs: Every summer, large numbers of people climb Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain. In 2026, the official climbing season opened on July 1, and once again, climbers had to follow strict rules designed to reduce overcrowding and improve safety.

The mountain has four main trails. In 2026, the Yoshida Trail in Yamanashi Prefecture and the Subashiri Trail in Shizuoka Prefecture opened on July 1, while the Fujinomiya and Gotemba trails, also in Shizuoka, opened on July 10. The season ended around September 10. Outside the official season, mountain huts and safety facilities are closed.

Climbers on all four trails had to pay a fee of 4,000 yen per person, the same amount as the previous year. In addition, they needed to make reservations. On the Yoshida Trail, which is the most popular, the number of climbers was limited to 4,000 per day, although people with reservations at mountain huts were not included in this limit. Climbers using the Shizuoka trails were also required to complete a short safety briefing before their climb.

Furthermore, the gates at the start of the trails were closed from about 2 p.m. to 3 a.m. for anyone without a mountain hut reservation. This rule aims to stop "bullet climbing," a dangerous practice in which people climb through the night without resting in order to reach the summit by sunrise. Such climbs can lead to altitude sickness and other health problems.

The rules were introduced because of concerns about overcrowding, accidents and damage to the environment. In 2023, for example, more than 220,000 people climbed the mountain during the summer season, and dozens of rescue operations were carried out in 2024. Local officials have also expressed concern about people who try to climb the mountain outside the official season, when conditions can be extremely dangerous. As a result, Yamanashi Prefecture has announced plans to require detailed climbing plans for people who want to climb during the closed season.
